title: A Low Frequency Vibration Energy Harvester Using ZnO Nanowires on Elastic Interdigitated Electrodes.

sections.heading: A Low Frequency Vibration Energy Harvester Using ZnO Nanowires on Elastic Interdigitated Electrodes
sections.text:
Byung-Rok Yoon, Jae-Hyoung Park, and Seung-Ki Lee∗ Department of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dankook University, Gyeonggi-do, 448-701, South Korea

This paper presents a low frequency piezoelectric vibration energy harvester using ZnO nanowires on elastic interdigitated electrodes. The interdigitated electrodes are formed using electroplated Ni and have suspended parts at the edges that are elastic and deformable by applying external force. A spherical Ni ball is used as a proof mass, which transforms a low frequency mechanical vibration into the force applied to deform the elastic electrodes. The ZnO nanowires are grown selectively on the electrodes and can generate a piezoelectric potential when the elastic electrodes are deformed by the proof mass activated by the external mechanical vibration. The proposed operation concept is demonstrated using two different types of energy harvesters, which have simple suspended part and cantilever array structures added to the electrodes, respectively. The output voltage of the fabricated harvesters is measured using a vibration exciter at $6 H z$ sinusoidal vibration with an acceleration of $0 . 5 ~ \mathfrak { g }$ . Maximum output power of 12.8 pW and 18.8 pW was generated with a load resistance of 1 M- for the harvesters using the simple suspended structure and cantilever array, respectively. Keywords: Low Frequency Piezoelectric Vibration Energy Harvester, ZnO Nanowires, Elastic Interdigitated Electrodes, Spherical Proof Mass.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Recently, harvesting electrical energy from mechanical vibration has been gaining substantial research momentum. The development of vibration energy harvesters in miniature or micro scale has been attracting attention owing mainly to the development of different batterypowered microelectronic devices and new fields of applications where the integration of a power source is becoming an obstacle for different reasons. Battery-powered portable devices, wireless sensor nodes for remote sensing, and implantable biomedical devices are valid examples.

Despite its abundance in nature, harvesting electrical energy from vibration is challenging for micro-electromechanical system (MEMS) devices as the amount of mechanical energy that can be transformed into electricity is typically extremely small. To maximize the energy conversion efficiency and power density of the harvesting device, to date, numerous approaches have been proposed. The three most widely used transduction mechanisms for MEMS transducers, piezoelectric, electromagnetic, and electrostatic mechanisms, have been researched for micro-power generation and energy harvesting.1- 2 Moreover, techniques such as resonance mode operation of spring-mass-damper-based systems and frequency upconversion have been utilized.3–5 Notwithstanding the efforts and successful implementation of some of the proposed concepts, harvesting energy from low frequency vibration remains a considerable challenge. Depending on the inherent nature of the vibration sources, humanbody-induced vibration for example, irregular and large amplitude vibrations at extremely low frequencies must be utilized in the applications. To overcome these issues, impact-based vibration energy harvesting and utilization of nonresonant power generation mechanisms have been researched.6–12 Ji et al. utilized an impact-induced vibration of a highly flexible piezoelectric material, Macro Fiber Composite (MFC), to generate power from low frequency vibrations.13 As the piezoelectric cantilever is vibrated in response to the impact between a freely movable proof mass and the housing, the output voltage of the piezoelectric cantilever is independent of the external vibration frequency. However, mechanical reliability issues in the contact region of the proof mass and housing must be overcome in these types of operation mechanisms.

In this research, we utilize the direct contact between a miniature scale spherical proof mass and zinc oxide $( Z \mathrm { n O } )$ nanowire to harvest energy from low frequency external vibration. ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires have been widely researched as a source of electric power generation; however, the utilization of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ in a miniature-scale harvesting device requires a means to deflect a large number of nanowires. Deflection of the substrate where the nanowire has been grown14–17 or brushing over the top surface of the nanowire has been proposed,18- 19 though an effective means to mechanically bend the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowire remains a challenge. Moreover, utilization of mechanical vibration to generate power from ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowire presents another obstacle to be overcome. We fabricate a flexible metal electrode array where ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires are grown selectively, on top of which a proof mass rolls in response to an external vibration. A proofof-concept device is fabricated and power generation characteristics are analyzed.

sections.heading: 2.1. Design of Energy Harvester
sections.text:
Figure 1 presents a schematic view of the proposed energy harvester and operation principle. The harvester is composed of a spherical proof mass and interdigitated elastic electrodes on which ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires are grown. The Copyright: Americainterdigitated electrodes are formed using electroplated Ni Delivereand have suspended parts at the edges that are elastic and deformable when an external force is applied. A spherical Ni ball with a diameter of $1 0 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ and mass of $1 5 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ is used as a proof mass, which transforms the low frequency mechanical vibration into the force to deform the elastic electrodes. The spherical proof mass is free to move on the electrodes and can convert a low frequency vibration into the force to deform the electrodes without using conventional resonant motion or the frequency up-conversion methods of spring-mass-based structures. The ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires are grown selectively on the electrodes and can generate a piezoelectric potential when subjected to an external force. The deformation of the elastic electrodes by the proof mass in response to the external mechanical vibration causes stress in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires, resulting in a piezoelectric potential generation along the length.

As the proof mass rolls or slides on the elastic electrodes, the suspended parts of the electrodes are deformed. When the proof mass moves toward the left side as indicated in Figure 1(b), the electrode on the left deforms downward and the suspended part of the electrode on the right side returns to its initial state. At this position, the asymmetry of the deformation on the electrodes can generate a piezoelectric potential difference between the two electrodes. Therefore, voltage and current pulses can be extracted through an external circuit when the proof mass moves between the electrodes because of the external mechanical vibration. Using this operation concept, stacked electrodes on top of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires and an additional intermediate insulating layer between the electrodes are not required.

Two different types of electrode structures are designed to compare the performances of the harvesters as displayed in Figure 2. The electrodes in Figure 2(a) have simple overhanging parts with the shape of eaves at the edges to be deformed by the movement of the proof mass. The width of the electrode is designed to be $2 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and the gap between the electrodes is $1 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The thickness of y Ingentathe electrodes is determined by the electroplating process of Ni and is designed to be $1 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The length of the suspended eaves at the edge of the electrode is $7 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , which is determined by the undercut etching process of the glass substrate. Compared with the electrodes in Figure 2(a), cantilever arrays have been added to the suspended parts to increase both the flexibility and effective deformable area of the electrodes as indicated in Figure 2(b). The width and length of the cantilever structure are 50 and $1 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. Harvesters with the proposed electrode structures were fabricated and tested.

sections.heading: 2.2. Fabrication of Energy Harvester
sections.text:
The overall fabrication process of the proposed harvester is displayed in Figure 3. Electrode structures of the harvester were formed on a $5 2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick Pyrex glass substrate. The interdigitated electrodes were fabricated by electroplating $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick Ni using a thick photoresist mold. A nickel sulfamate-based electrolyte was used as the electroplating solution. Direct current was applied with a current density of $5 \ \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . The electroplating mold and seed layer were removed to reveal the glass substrate around the Ni electrodes. The glass substrate was isotropically etched with diluted hydrogen fluoride (HF) solution and undercut below the electrode forms suspended and deformable structure at the edges. The isotropic undercut etching process determined the length of the suspended part, which is $5 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ .

![](images/d5d0f8e9a8089b3bc9a479736220a7291a43f72de8ac538d7b0ba47a8797abdc.jpg)  
Figure 3. Overall fabrication process.

![](images/3ebd66355e9abe1d37fa254e59b30615e78be6207c5b29339b97e3a30a935b3c.jpg)  
Figure 4. Scanning electron microscopy images of: (a) Interdigitated elastic electrodes; (b) electrodes with cantilever array; (c) magnified view of the electrode on which $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ nanowires are selectively grown; (d) side view of $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ nanowires grown on patterned seed layer.

A ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ seed layer was patterned for the selective growth of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ IP: 146.185.201.152 On:nanowires on the electrodes. ZnO nanowires must Deliverebe formed only on the electrodes for the isolation between electrodes. We utilized a cost-effective hydrothermal growth method as the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires can be easily grown on a large surface area and scaled up at low temperature.20 Further, ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires can be grown selectively on the patterned seed layer using the hydrothermal growth method. To pattern the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ seed layer on the electrodes, a lift-off process was used. As indicated in Figure 3(d), negative photoresist was coated on the entire surface and exposed with an ultra violet (UV) light source through the transparent glass substrate from the backside. The Ni electrode prevents the photoresist coated on the surface from UV exposure, which enables the self-alignment of the photoresist pattern with the electrode without an y Ingentaadditional mask. In the subsequent development process, only the photoresist on the Ni electrodes is removed. After the photoresist development, a $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ seed layer was sputtered with a substrate temperature of $1 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ seed layer around the electrodes was selectively removed during the lift-off process displayed in Figure $3 ( \mathrm { g } )$ , followed by a thermal annealing process at $3 6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $6 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ . Finally, ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires were grown in an aqueous mixture solution of $0 . 1 \textbf { M }$ zinc nitrate hexahydrate and hexamethylenetetramine with an equimolar ratio at 85 C for eight hours.

![](images/1816ca29e73d13a1ad66a1471aecd42fd3b6b55e56032ec63dfbb15ade86b03b.jpg)  
Figure 5. Measured average length and diameter of $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ nanowires according to growth time: (a) Length; (b) diameter.

Figure 4 displays the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the fabricated piezoelectric energy harvesters with elastic electrodes. When the etching depth of the glass substrate was $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the observed lateral undercut was $7 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ , which was the length of suspended parts of the electrodes with the shape of eaves. As indicated in Figure 4(b), the cantilever structures were completely released from the substrate in the isotropic glass etching process. Figure 4(c) displays the edge of one electrode where ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires were grown. ZnO nanowires were selectively grown on the entire electrode surface, whereas virtually no nanowires were observed on the glass substrate. A side view of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires grown on the planar surface is displayed in Figure 4(d). The length and diameter are proportionally increased with hydrothermal growth time. Figure 5 indicates the measured average length and diameter of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires grown on the patterned seed layer according to growth time. With a growth time of eight hours in the aqueous solution, the measured average length and diameter were approximately $3 . 7 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ , respectively.

sections.heading: 3.1. Experimental Configuration
sections.text:
Fabricated piezoelectric energy harvesters with two dif-Copyright: Americaferent types of electrode structures were tested using a Deliverevibration exciter (Bruel and Kjær LDS V406) at different mechanical vibration frequencies and accelerations. The fabricated device was mounted on the exciter to induce an in-plane motion of the spherical proof mass on the electrodes in response to the external vibration. To ensure a straight-line motion of the proof mass on the electrodes, the fabricated electrode and proof mass were assembled using an acrylic guiding jig. A schematic diagram of the assembly using the guiding jig is displayed in Figure 6. Figure 7(a) illustrates the energy harvester assembled with the acrylic jig; the assembled device mounted on the vibration exciter is displayed in Figure 7(b).

The vibration exciter was driven by a sinusoidal signal generated with a function generator and amplified with a power amplifier. To verify the feasibility of the harvesting energy from low frequency vibrations, the output voltage of the fabricated device was measured at $6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ sinusoidal vibration with an acceleration of $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . A digital oscilloscope was employed to record the output voltage of the energy harvester subjected to the vibration.

sections.heading: 3.2. Measurements and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 8 displays the open circuit voltage waveform of the energy harvester having a simple suspended part on the electrodes as indicated in Figure 2(a), when the device was subjected to a $6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ sinusoidal vibration with an acceleration of $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . As the external vibration is controlled by a sinusoidal signal, the spherical proof mass moves faster at the center of the device and slows near both ends of the device. The inset in Figure 8 represents the schematic view of the proof mass vibration. The measured open circuit output voltage waveform corresponds to the output generated by the motion of the proof mass subjected to an external vibration. At a vibration frequency of $6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ it requires approximately 83 msec for the proof mass to travel from one end to the other inside the guiding jig, which corresponds to the period of the measured output voltage waveform.

![](images/051a9ba012b0129650f7d46f4d8896a7ef380cd63bf4c0ab84ac427a8e4b89c6.jpg)  
Figure 6. Schematic view of assembly using guiding jig.

Figure 9 displays the open circuit output voltage waveforms for two different types of energy harvesters having a y Ingentasimple suspended structure and a cantilever array. The positive and negative pulses repeat regularly with a period of approximately 1.4 msec as indicated in the zoomed view of the open circuit output voltage waveform. The results indicate that it requires approximately 1.4 msec for the spherical proof mass to pass through one pair of interdigitated electrodes. The positive output pulse is recorded when the proof mass moves to the edge of one electrode; the negative pulse appears when the proof mass passes through the opposing electrode, which verifies that a low frequency vibration can be well-transformed into a potential difference between the two electrodes. Maximum peak-to-peak open circuit voltage of $2 6 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ was obtained for the harvester with a simple suspended part on the electrode; the harvester using a cantilever array structure demonstrated maximum peak-to-peak open circuit voltage of $3 6 ~ \mathrm { m V } .$

The average power delivered to an external resistive load is compared in Figure 10. The load resistance was varied from 0.5 to $8 \ : \mathrm { M } \Omega$ and the average power delivered to each resistive load was calculated using the following equation:

$$
P = { \frac { 1 } { T } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } { \frac { v ( t ) ^ { 2 } } { R } } d t = { \frac { V _ { \mathrm { r m s } } ^ { 2 } } { R } }
$$

where $T$ , $v ( t ) , R$ , and $V _ { \mathrm { r m s } }$ are the period, instantaneous output voltage, load resistance, and root mean square (RMS) value of the output voltage, respectively. For both harvesters, the maximum average power was obtained with a load resistance of $1 \ \mathrm { ~ M } \Omega$ . The maximum output power of the harvester using a simple suspended structure was $1 2 . 8 \mathrm { \ p W }$ ; the harvester with a cantilever array structure generated a maximum power of $1 8 . 8 \ \mathrm { p W }$

![](images/f5aa6e3b0c46fa95408d839188943efaacee105be2e0a8b4cdeb984c347bea7b.jpg)  
Figure 7. (a) Energy harvester and proof mass assembled with acrylic jig; (b) assembled device mounted on vibration exciter.

![](images/79fea12da631a241d370fbaa32517f10c99e4b7c392490e4b4919e5af7668d1d.jpg)  
Figure 8. Open circuit output voltage waveform of energy harvester at $6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ sinusoidal vibration with acceleration of $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ .

The improvement of the open circuit output voltage and average power with the cantilever array structure can be attributed to the increase of flexibility and effective deformable area in the interdigitated electrodes. The measured open circuit voltage and average power were relatively small compared with conventional piezoelectric energy harvesters based on the bending motion of cantilever-type piezoelectric materials. This result can be ascribed to the small amount of acceleration during vibration, which was $0 . 5 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ in the experiment. However, the proposed low frequency vibration harvester concept was Scientific Publishersdemonstrated with elastic interdigitated electrodes and y Ingentaspherical proof mass. An improvement of the power conversion efficiency can be expected with further optimization of the elastic interdigitated electrodes with appropriate gap and suspended height. Moreover, the utilization of a flexible substrate can potentially be useful in increasing the contact area between the proof mass and ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowire. A cylindrical rod instead of a spherical ball as a proof mass can be applied to enhance the power generation by increasing the electrode deformation area. The guiding jig used in assembling the spherical proof mass and interdigitated electrodes must be further improved with a low surface friction on the sidewall and high restitution force at both ends to enhance the power conversion efficiency.

![](images/c9a1009c5e00b169164a4c906a1b9445a86ecfb75fc3815d6dbe3d93502ee7a4.jpg)

![](images/94af79e5968b4013e0db4375368089894101e4eff8d2d789949a309265a29354.jpg)  
Figure 10. Average power delivered to external resistive load for two different types of energy harvesters.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSION
sections.text:
In this research, we designed, fabricated, and tested piezoelectric energy harvesters using ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires selectively grown on elastic interdigitated electrodes and a spheri-IP: 146.185.201.152 On:cal proof mass moving on the electrodes that converts Copyright: Americalow frequency mechanical vibration into electric energy. DelivereAs the spherical proof mass vibrates on the interdigitated electrodes, it simultaneously causes the mechanical deformation of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires-grown electrodes. The deformation of the electrodes generates electric power from the piezoelectric potential in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires. All the components of the harvesters were formed on a planar substrate. Moreover, neither a stacked electrode on top of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ nanowires nor an additional intermediate insulating layers between electrodes was required. Using a spherical proof mass that was free to move on the electrodes, the low frequency mechanical vibration could be transformed into electric power generation, without the use of conventional resonant motion or frequency up-conversion methods of spring-mass-based structures. Measurement results confirm that the proposed concept of a piezoelectric energy harvester was successfully demonstrated.
